migrationNotes: Spine: push a supermarket trolley, empty and then loaded. Turn what the push feels like into a = F ÷ m, follow a cart whose net force points against its motion, then work the rule backwards for a force or a mass.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-force-mass-acceleration-2 (the verbal doubling item, covered by the opening screen and the hook).

lesson.title: Force, mass and acceleration

steps.headline: The empty trolley and the loaded one

lead.text: Take a supermarket trolley of mass 5 kg and push it with a steady 10 N. Its velocity rises by 2 m/s every second, so its acceleration is 2 m/s². Now load it until its mass is 10 kg, which is twice as much. Push with the same 10 N and the loaded trolley is harder to get moving. Its velocity rises by only 1 m/s every second. Doubling the mass halved the acceleration.

Go back to the empty trolley and push twice as hard, with 20 N. Now it speeds up by 4 m/s every second, so doubling the push doubled the acceleration. The direction matters too. The trolley speeds up the way you push, so the acceleration points the way the force points.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares the three trolleys. Two patterns show in it. The acceleration grows in step with the force and shrinks in step with the mass. The next screen turns both into a single rule.

lead.text: Loading the trolley changes its mass and leaves the push alone.

reveal.text: Twice the mass with the same push gives half the acceleration, so 6 ÷ 2.

lead.text: Both patterns fit a single rule: the acceleration equals the net force divided by the mass. This is Newton's second law of motion. In symbols it is a = F ÷ m, where F is the net force, m is the mass and a is the acceleration. It is more often written F = ma, which says the same thing.

The rule is also where the newton comes from. A net force of 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². The 5 kg trolley fits: 10 N ÷ 5 kg = 2 m/s². The rule needs the net force, so when several forces act on an object they are first added with their signs, and only the total is divided by the mass. A positive net force gives a positive acceleration. A net force of zero gives an acceleration of zero, which is the balanced case from the last lesson.
A 3 kg cart has two horizontal forces on it, one pointing right and one pointing left. Right is positive.

reveal.text: You found the net force first, then divided by the mass. That is the second law at work.

steps.headline: A trolley of mass 8 kg has 30 N right and 6 N left on it. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: Find the net force. The leftward force is negative.
Divide the net force by the mass.
The sign is positive, so the acceleration points right.

steps.headline: A net force of 24 N pushes a 2 kg cart to the right. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The force given is already the net force.
Divide the net force by the mass.

steps.headline: The acceleration follows the net force

lead.text: The rule says nothing about which way the object is moving, only about the net force on it. Take a 2 kg cart rolling to the right at 5 m/s, with a 10 N force acting to the left. The net force is −10 N, so the acceleration is −10 ÷ 2 = −5 m/s². The cart is still moving right, but each second its velocity falls by 5 m/s. After one second it is stationary, and after that it starts to move left.

This is the pattern from the lesson on changing velocity, and now we can say what causes it. If the velocity and the net force point the same way, the object speeds up. If they point opposite ways it slows down, and if the force keeps acting it eventually reverses. Braking is the everyday case: the net force on the car points backwards while the car moves forwards.
A 4 kg cart moves right at 6 m/s. A 4 N force pushes it right and a 12 N force pushes it left.

reveal.text: The acceleration follows the net force. The cart is still going right, and it is slowing down.

steps.headline: Finding the force or the mass

lead.text: The rule can be turned round. Sometimes the acceleration is known and the force is what we want. A 5 kg trolley that has to speed up at 3 m/s² needs a net force of F = ma = 5 × 3 = 15 N.

Sometimes the force and the acceleration are known and the mass is the unknown. Dividing both sides of F = ma by a gives m = F ÷ a. A net force of 30 N that produces an acceleration of 6 m/s² is acting on a mass of 30 ÷ 6 = 5 kg. Pushing something and watching how fast it speeds up is a way to find its mass without putting it on a scale.

The rule also compares objects. For the same acceleration, a larger mass needs a larger net force, because F = ma grows with m. Pushing a loaded trolley up to the same acceleration as an empty one takes more effort.
Now the other way round: the mass and the acceleration are known, and the net force is not.

reveal.text: Net force is mass times acceleration, so the force is 4 × 3 newtons.

lesson.orientation: Use net force and mass to predict how velocity changes.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You push an empty supermarket trolley across a car park. It gets going quickly, and a few seconds later you are walking briskly beside it. Now load it with a week's shopping and push just as hard. It gets going more slowly. Ask a friend to push alongside you, and it speeds up faster again.

You have felt this many times, and each time it says something about the trolley's acceleration, the rate at which its velocity changes. A bigger push gives more acceleration and a bigger load gives less. The last lesson showed what happens when the pushes and pulls on an object cancel. This one is about what happens when they do not.

We start with the trolley and turn the feeling into a short rule with numbers. Then we use the rule to find an acceleration from a push and to follow a cart that is slowing down. The last step works backwards from an acceleration to the force or the mass behind it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use net force and mass to find acceleration, and work the other way to find a force or a mass.

recap.keyIdea: The net force equals mass times acceleration: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less. The acceleration points the way the net force points.

blocks.text: You saw the same push on twice the mass give half the acceleration, 3 m/s² instead of 6. You found that a cart moving right can accelerate to the left when the net force points that way, and that a net force of 12 N gives a 4 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s².

recap.nextHook: A book on a table has gravity pulling on it, yet the book does not accelerate. Next we find what balances that pull and what it takes to hold something up.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart has horizontal forces of 18 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: Add the forces before applying the second law.
Divide the net force by mass.
Calculate (18 − 6)/3.
questions.onCorrect: 4 m/s². Add the forces to get the net force, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the net force. Divide it by the mass to get the acceleration.
That divides one force by the mass. Use the net force of both.

questions.prompt: The mass doubles while the net force stays the same. What happens to acceleration?
hints: Keep the numerator fixed in a = F_net/m.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

questions.onCorrect: It is halved. The same net force spread over twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger mass is harder to accelerate, not easier. Mass is on the bottom of a = F ÷ m.
Mass is in the formula, so changing it changes the acceleration.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart experiences a net force of 24 N rightward. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: The stated force is already the net force.
Use acceleration = net force divided by mass.
Divide the stated net force by the cart's mass.
questions.onCorrect: 12 m/s². The force given is already the net force, so divide it by the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. To find acceleration, divide the force by the mass.
That subtracts the mass. Divide the force by it.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving right has forces of 4 N right and 12 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: The velocity does not change the force sum.
Subtract the leftward force and divide by mass.
Calculate (4 − 12)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s². The net force is leftward, so the acceleration is leftward whatever way the cart is moving.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the larger force points left. The acceleration is negative.
That drops the 4 N rightward force. Both forces count towards the net force.

questions.prompt: What net force, in newtons, gives a 4 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?
hints: This time, the mass and acceleration are known.
Multiply them to find net force.
Calculate 4 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. Net force is mass times acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides acceleration by mass. To find a force, multiply them.
That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A heavier cart and a lighter cart must have the same acceleration. Which needs the larger net force?
hints: Hold acceleration fixed in the second law.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.

choices.label: Both need the same net force

questions.onCorrect: The heavier cart. For the same acceleration, F = ma grows with the mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The lighter cart needs less force for the same acceleration, because it has less mass to move.
Mass sets how much force a given acceleration needs, so the two carts differ.

questions.prompt: The same push makes an empty trolley speed up by 6 m/s each second. By how much per second does it speed up when it is loaded to twice the mass? Give the acceleration in m/s².
hints: Is the loaded trolley easier or harder to speed up?
Twice the mass to move with the same push.
Share the 6 m/s over two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twice the mass, same push: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s each second.

questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². The same push on twice the mass gives half the acceleration, as the second law says.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the acceleration. A loaded trolley is harder to speed up, not easier.

questions.prompt: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg cart. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Is the force given the net force?
Use acceleration = net force ÷ mass.
Share the 20 N across the 4 kg.
questions.onCorrect: 5 m/s². Acceleration is net force divided by mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide to get acceleration.
That subtracts the mass from the force. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: Why is 24 N, not 30 N, divided by the mass?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.

choices.label: Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.
The trolley ignores the larger force.

questions.onCorrect: The second law uses the net force. Opposing forces cancel before you divide.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is in kilograms and is given separately. 24 N is a force.
Both forces count. The leftward one takes away from the rightward one.

questions.prompt: A net force of 45 N gives an object an acceleration of 9 m/s². What is its mass in kg?
hints: The second law links force, mass and acceleration.
Mass is net force divided by acceleration.
Share the 45 N over each 9 m/s².
questions.onCorrect: 5 kg. Rearranging F = ma gives m = F ÷ a.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by acceleration. Divide the force by the acceleration.
That divides acceleration by force. Put the force on top.

citations.claim: For a given net force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration, and doubling the force doubles it; the acceleration points the way the force points.
Twice the mass with the same push gives half the acceleration: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s².
Newton's second law: the net force equals mass times acceleration, a = F ÷ m, and 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
A 3 kg cart with 18 N right and 6 N left has a net force of 12 N and an acceleration of 4 m/s².
An 8 kg trolley with 30 N right and 6 N left has a net force of 24 N and an acceleration of 3 m/s².
A net force of 24 N on a 2 kg cart gives an acceleration of 12 m/s².
The acceleration points the way the net force points, whatever way the object is moving; a net force against the motion slows it.
A 4 kg cart moving right with 4 N right and 12 N left has an acceleration of (4 − 12) ÷ 4 = −2 m/s².
Rearranging F = ma gives F = ma and m = F ÷ a; for the same acceleration a larger mass needs a larger net force.
A 4 kg object accelerating at 3 m/s² needs a net force of 4 × 3 = 12 N.
For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.
Twice the mass, same push: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s each second.
Only the net force counts, so the 6 N leftward force is taken off first.
